documents.title: ICCS practical guidelines clinical flow cytometry

chunks.content: 1 Introduction The diagnosis of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH) relies on detecting the loss of the glycosyl‐phosphatidyl inositol (GPI)‐anchored surface molecules from both white blood cells (WBCs) and red blood cells (RBCs) by flow cytometry [ , , ], despite the underlying molecular mechanism involving somatic mutations of the X‐linked phosphatidyl‐inositol glycan Class A ( PIGA ) gene [ , ]. Significant progress has been made since the use of the FLAER reagent [ , ] and the publication of international recommendations [ , , , , ]. Various sizes of the PNH clone, consisting of totally deficient cells (type III) alone or associated with partially deficient cells (type II) [ ], can be quantified by flow cytometry. The International PNH Interest Group (IPIG) has classified disease with PNH clones into three subtypes: classical PNH, which includes hemolytic and thrombotic patients who have evidence of PNH clones in the absence of another bone marrow failure disorder; PNH in the context of other primary bone marrow disorders, such as aplastic anemia and myelodysplastic neoplasms; and subclinical PNH, in which patients have small PNH clones but no clinical or laboratory evidence of hemolysis or thrombosis [ ]. Patients with classical PNH typically have higher clone sizes in WBCs; monocyte and neutrophil clone sizes classically correlate well at the time of diagnosis than patients in other categories; these patients also, by definition, have evidence of hemolysis in the form of elevated LDH and reticulocyte counts. RBC clone sizes, however, are less reliable as these are typically lower in untreated patients with PNH due to hemolysis and/or transfusion. Importantly, the size of the neutrophil clone is relevant to the thrombosis risk for the classical PNH patient [ ]. Patients with subclinical PNH have the smallest clone sizes of any of the IPIG classification groups [ , , , , , ]. Early diagnosis of PNH is essential for providing optimal care and treatment if clinically indicated [ , , , , ]. Since flow cytometry is the gold standard to detect PNH clones, performing the assay on fresh cells is crucial to ensure high‐quality results. Therefore, the French PNH working group, initiated in 2010 after the publication of the first international recommendations [ ], aimed to harmonize diagnostic practices throughout the country. First, a dedicated workshop was conducted to evaluate different flow cytometry methods in a multiplatform and multicenter approach. Then, we developed in 2013 a quality control scheme for the French‐speaking region based on the international recommendations for PNH screening [ ]. This interlaboratory comparison program is still ongoing, and we report here on our group's 10‐year experience, during which we successfully built a strong network of cytometrists. 2 2010—The Start With a Dedicated Workshop for <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Testing on <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">WBCs</styled-content> In 2010, the first publication of the international recommendations highlighted the relevance of a new reagent for flow cytometry called FLAER, an inactivated bacterial toxin able to bind to all GPI‐anchored proteins on leucocytes and to detect their deficiency [ , , ]. In order to share these guidelines, the French PNH working group was established in 2010. Inspired by the General de Gaulle's famous “18th of June Call,” we initiated a dedicated workshop following our call on June 18, 2010, marking the first French‐speaking meeting focused on PNH diagnosis and high‐sensitivity assays in WBCs. Thirty‐five French and Belgian laboratories participated in this multicenter study aimed at evaluating various flow cytometry methods for PNH testing on WBCs across multiple platforms. 2.1 Succeeding in Multicenter Instrument Harmonization The 35 centers were equipped with multiparameter flow cytometers including 8‐color/3‐laser FACSCanto II (BD Biosciences, San Jose CA, USA) in 14 laboratories, 5‐color/1‐laser FC500 (Beckman‐Coulter, Miami FL, USA) in 13 laboratories, and 10‐color/3‐laser Navios (Beckman‐Coulter) in 8 laboratories. The harmonization of the instrument settings was achieved in the 18 centers outfitted with 3‐laser flow cytometers using 8‐peak Rainbow bead calibration particles, after conversion of the fluorescent intensity target values [ ] (Figure ). As an illustration, the coefficients of variation (CVs) were below 5% for FITC, PE, PerCP‐Cy5.5/PC5.5, APC, and V450/PB fluorescence channels, yet slightly increased for the PE‐Cy7 channel to 5.7%, as expected [ ]. 2.2 Achieving a 10<sup>−4</sup> Limit of Detection in a Harmonized Multicenter Approach In order to investigate the technical limit of PNH testing in a multicenter approach, the participating centers were asked to perform three different staining procedures on WBCs, after implementing the harmonization described above. Two‐color (CD11b/CD55‐CD59 [ ]) and 6‐color combinations, including or not the FLAER reagent (FLAER/CD24/CD14/CD33/CD15/CD45 or CD55/CD24/CD14/CD33/CD15/CD45 in one or two tubes depending on the cytometer type) were proposed. At that time, neither panel option included CD64 for monocyte gating. The gating strategy used was the one recommended by the international guidelines [ ]. in a Harmonized Multicenter Approach In order to investigate the technical limit of PNH testing in a multicenter approach, the participating centers were asked to perform three different staining procedures on WBCs, after implementing the harmonization described above. Two‐color (CD11b/CD55‐CD59 [ ]) and 6‐color combinations, including or not the FLAER reagent (FLAER/CD24/CD14/CD33/CD15/CD45 or CD55/CD24/CD14/CD33/CD15/CD45 in one or two tubes depending on the cytometer type) were proposed. At that time, neither panel option included CD64 for monocyte gating. The gating strategy used was the one recommended by the international guidelines [ ]. The purpose of that workshop was to develop a high‐sensitivity test dedicated to WBCs in a harmonized multicenter approach. In this study, the minimal requirements for defining a PNH population were the observation of at least 20 events with total absence of GPI‐linked protein expression (type III cells). Hence, all participants were asked to acquire a minimum of 200,000 neutrophils in order to reach the optimal limit of detection. Three hundred and five peripheral blood samples were obtained from 75 locally diagnosed PNH patients (PNH clones ranging from 0.08% to 99.95%), 62 patients with circulating immature granulocytes, and 41 patients with MDS, as well as 127 controls. The initial results gathered from in‐house gating strategies highlighted the need for harmonized procedures and participant education, which were subsequently implemented. A higher cellular background was observed in MDS samples and in those with immature granulocytes. By employing harmonized multiparametric approaches with both 6‐color combinations and harmonized gating strategies procedures across multiplatforms, we achieved a 10 −4 limit of detection [ ]. For robust quantification of minor PNH clones, the use of the FLAER is recommended [ ]. This reagent was included in all the files generated for our interlaboratory comparison program (see below). 3 2013–2024—Highlights From the 10‐Year Experience of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Interlaboratory Comparison Program The insights gained from the workshop highlighted that, for PNH diagnosis by flow cytometry, both technical proficiency and the accuracy of interpretation and reporting are equally critical. UK NEQAS for Leucocyte Immunophenotyping proposes stabilized samples for PNH in their External Quality Assessment (EQA) programs [ , ]. However, there was a need for a French‐speaking program, particularly for the report drafting. Therefore, we have developed since 2013 a quality control scheme for the French‐speaking region, aligned with the first international guidelines for PNH screening [ ]. This program aims to improve PNH diagnosis practices by analyzing the three recommended different populations in peripheral blood: neutrophils, monocytes, and RBCs. 3.1 Proposing a Two‐Step Survey Program We propose a 1‐year, two‐step survey program to any volunteering clinical laboratories from French‐speaking countries [ ]. It consists of running two successive surveys: a virtual survey based on raw data file analysis to harmonize data interpretation and quality of reports, and a second survey based on a fresh whole‐blood sample analysis to examine the whole process, from the technical procedure to the final report, and appreciate the employed methods in the participating laboratories. Regarding virtual cases, raw data files sent to the centers are currently generated simultaneously by different cytometers: BD Biosciences instruments (BD FACSCanto II and FACSLyric, this latter being used since 2021) and Beckman Coulter instruments (Navios and DxFLEX, this latter being used since 2023). In the context of the fresh survey, whole blood samples are provided by Dr. Bernard Drenou (Groupe Hospitalier de la Région Mulhouse Sud Alsace) in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and participants are asked to use their own routine flow cytometric procedures immediately after reception. Following the international guidelines [ ], participants are instructed to report the PNH clone size as follows: only the total PNH clone size in both the WBCs (neutrophils and monocytes) should be included in the conclusion, alongside the percentage of type II and type III RBCs and the total RBC clone size. In France, data on type II and type III percentages in WBCs are also collected, along with type II and type III percentages in RBCs, due to the establishment of the National Observatory of PNH clones. It is important to note that in cases where there is no clear distinction between PNH type II and type III RBCs, it is recommended to report a combined population of RBCs with CD59 deficiency, accompanied by a comment explaining the reason, rather than setting arbitrary regions for type II and type III [ ]. For the statistical analysis of the participant results, a robust statistical method is used in compliance with the ISO/International Electrotechnical Commission 17043 [ ] requirement concerning the proficiency of the interlaboratory quality controllers. Robust mean, coefficient of variation (CV), standard deviation (SD), and z score are calculated for type II, type III, and total PNH cell subsets across the three analyzed lineages (neutrophils, monocytes, and RBCs). These metrics are provided to

report a combined population of RBCs with CD59 deficiency, accompanied by a comment explaining the reason, rather than setting arbitrary regions for type II and type III [ ]. For the statistical analysis of the participant results, a robust statistical method is used in compliance with the ISO/International Electrotechnical Commission 17043 [ ] requirement concerning the proficiency of the interlaboratory quality controllers. Robust mean, coefficient of variation (CV), standard deviation (SD), and z score are calculated for type II, type III, and total PNH cell subsets across the three analyzed lineages (neutrophils, monocytes, and RBCs). These metrics are provided to each participant in a private report for both virtual and fresh cases with a PNH clone. In case where no PNH clone is detected, only the robust mean, CV, and SD of the number of analyzed cells are provided, along with the assay sensitivity for the three different lineages included. All private reports incorporate a standard interpretation of the results developed by the group of experts. Eventually, the participants also receive a general report on each of the two different surveys [ ]. 3.2 Demonstrating the Strong Commitment From French‐Speaking Laboratories Throughout the 10‐Year Program The first 2013 edition of the interlaboratory comparison program succeeded in rallying 49 participants from voluntary centers [ ]. Over the last 10 years, the number of participants slightly increased (Figure ), achieving nearly 60 participants in 2023, including the four expert centers: 50 French metropolitan, one French overseas, four Belgian, one Swiss, and one Moroccan (Figure ). This demonstrates a strong commitment from the registered centers throughout the program duration. We believe that this participant engagement relies on both the quality of the flow cytometry files provided and the diverse PNH clinical situations that illustrate “real‐life” issues. Over the past 10 years, nine fresh cases (FC) were provided to the participants (Figure ), featuring various clone sizes across the three lineages, ranging from 0.15% to 98.8% on neutrophils. We collected the mean and the coefficient of variation for each survey (Table ). Regardless of the lineage, smaller clone sizes are associated with a wider coefficient of variation. Notably, the percentage of type II RBCs, ranging from 0.03% to 7.42%, is often associated with a very large coefficient of variation, highlighting the challenges in delineating this cell type, as it has been elegantly recently demonstrated [ ]. 3.3 Offering Insights Into Various <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Clinical Situations The interlaboratory comparison program has evolved over the last 10 years, particularly to align with the revised international guidelines [ , , , ]. New panels for WBC analysis of virtual cases were proposed, notably for monocyte gating. CD64 has been defined as the recommended non‐GPI linked marker for monocyte identification instead of CD33. Therefore, we chose to modify in 2019 the staining of the samples used for the virtual cases and have since proposed panels that include either CD64 or CD33. However, we decided not to implement CD157, despite its potential to replace both CD24 and CD14 [ ], since several CD157‐negative, non‐PNH cases have been reported [ ]. Besides, owing to the strong emphasis placed on the RBC analysis in the revised recommendations, we proposed cases focusing on the importance of studying that lineage. Indeed, we proposed a virtual case involving a 70‐year‐old woman with aplastic anemia. The assay sensitivity on monocytes did not allow for a conclusion, while GPI‐deficient cells were detected in neutrophils and estimated at 0.15%. In this case, analysis on RBCs proved invaluable, as it confirmed the presence of a PNH clone with a size of 0.04% ( the figures indicated were obtained using the FACSCanto II cytometer, see Figure , upper panels). Another virtual case highlighted the interest of the PNH clone size quantification on RBCs. It involved a 30‐year‐old man diagnosed with classical PNH, presenting a major PNH clone at 93.12% on neutrophils and 94.2% on monocytes, and 33.00% on RBCs at diagnosis. The files sent to the participants corresponded to the 1‐year follow‐up during eculizumab treatment [ ]. The clone size slightly increased on WBCs (96.99% on neutrophils and 95.9% on monocytes; the figures indicated were obtained using the FACSCanto II cytometer, see Figure , upper panels). An expected increase in size to 92.56% was observed in RBCs, indicating successful therapy, as eculizumab prevents hemolysis of the GPI‐deficient PNH RBCs [ ]. Among the 20 surveys, we challenged the participants with the case of a 57‐year‐old woman with aplastic anemia who underwent bone marrow transplantation. The PNH clone, initially estimated at 1.40% on neutrophils, 7.1% on monocytes, and 0.36% on RBCs at diagnosis ( the figures indicated were obtained using the Navios cytometer, see Figure , lower panels), disappeared in the follow‐up sample (Figure ). 3.4 Improving Practices in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Diagnosis Since reporting is a crucial part

increase in size to 92.56% was observed in RBCs, indicating successful therapy, as eculizumab prevents hemolysis of the GPI‐deficient PNH RBCs [ ]. Among the 20 surveys, we challenged the participants with the case of a 57‐year‐old woman with aplastic anemia who underwent bone marrow transplantation. The PNH clone, initially estimated at 1.40% on neutrophils, 7.1% on monocytes, and 0.36% on RBCs at diagnosis ( the figures indicated were obtained using the Navios cytometer, see Figure , lower panels), disappeared in the follow‐up sample (Figure ). 3.4 Improving Practices in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PNH</styled-content> Diagnosis Since reporting is a crucial part of the process, we created a compact guide designed to fit in a laboratory coat pocket, aimed at harmonizing PNH test conclusions in accordance with the successive international recommendations [ , , , , ]. We analyzed the conformity of the final reports provided by the participants in cases of both PNH clone presence (Figure ) and absence (Figure ). Over the past 10 years, we have proudly observed a significant increase in conformity for both clinical situations, reaching 96%. 3.5 Towards the Next Workshop Dedicated to <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">RBC</styled-content> Assay The initial workshop we conducted played a crucial role in the harmonization of PNH testing in France. While we focused on implementing WBC analysis for PNH testing, there is now a pressing need to improve the RBC assay. We are planning to organize a dedicated workshop in 2025 to present the newly developed screening test involving immature RBCs (iRBCs) [ ]. Indeed, the PNH clone size evaluated in CD71+ RBCs appears to be larger than in mature RBCs and correlates with that in both neutrophils and monocytes [ ]. The major advantage of the CD71 addition is the more reliable separation between true PNH type II and PNH type III cells versus the incorrect inclusion of transfused cells into the PNH RBC clone. The reason for the almost identical PNH clone size between the lineages is that the iRBCs are not prone to complement‐mediated lysis. Moreover, detection of C3d deposit on RBCs by flow cytometry in anti‐C5‐treated patients may be of interest for assessing extravascular hemolysis [ ]. 4 A Strong Network of Cytometrists Built in France Following the diagnostic practice harmonization spread in France since 2013 through our ongoing inter‐laboratory comparison program, our PNH working group initiated a nationwide multicenter prospective observational study on February 29, 2016, in order to collect all PNH cases or GPI‐deficient cells above 0.01%. The first main objective is to monitor the long‐term evolution of minor PNH clones < 1%, which represent over one third of positive samples [ ], using high‐resolution flow cytometry, as previous evaluations showed the disappearance of PNH clones in 6%–24% of patients with bone marrow failure over 3–5 years with a 2‐color flow cytometry procedure [ , ]. The second objective aims to further investigate the relevance of classifying type II and type III PNH cells in WBCs in clones larger than 1%, as the significance of this distinction—unlike in RBCs—remains unclear. The collected data at diagnosis and during long‐term follow‐up are currently under analysis. This experience and the strong network of cytometrists we have built since the workshop conducted in 2010 led us to create in 2018 the French‐speaking flow cytometry association in Hematology, namely the CytHem for Cytometry in Hematology ( https://www.cythem.fr ). Its main purpose is to harmonize the diagnostic practices by sharing technical protocols and gating strategies for the different instruments equipping the routine laboratories. Eleven working groups have been created, each dedicated to a specific hemopathy or disease group (PNH, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, acute myeloid leukemia, mature B‐cell neoplasms, central nervous lymphomas, granular lymphocytic leukemia, lymphoblastic leukemia, Sezary Syndrome, plasma cell neoplasms), except CytHem‐questions, which was established to address practical issues, provide information, and manage In Vitro Diagnosis Regulations (IVDR) concerns. Each disease working group is closely related to a French‐speaking clinical association. The PNH working group is indeed working alongside the rare immuno‐hematological diseases (MaRIH) healthcare network ( https://marih.fr ). Author Contributions O.W‐.B. designed the study and wrote the manuscript, M.L.G‐.T. led the workshop, initiated the French working group, and helped write the manuscript, R.L. led the workshop and initiated the French working group, B.D. led the workshop, initiated the French working group, and provided whole blood samples for the interlaboratory comparison program, and A.D. is in charge of the interlaboratory comparison program, draws figures, and helped write the manuscript. Ethics Statement For the workshop, informed consent forms were collected in compliance with the regulations of the ethical committee of each institution; for the interlaboratory comparison program, whole blood samples are provided in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. documents.title: ICCS Standardization Document Voiding Dysfunction Pediatric

chunks.content: Introduction Overactive bladder (OAB) represents one of the most prevalent and clinically significant pediatric urological conditions, affecting approximately 5–12% of children aged 5–10 years worldwide [ ]. According to the International Children’s Continence Society, pediatric OAB is defined as urinary urgency, typically with frequency and nocturia, with or without urinary incontinence, occurring without urinary tract infection or other obvious pathology [ ]. Pediatric OAB presents as a complex set of urinary symptoms that impact children and families [ ]. Symptoms include increased daytime frequency, an urgent need to urinate with holding maneuvers, daytime accidents, and nocturnal enuresis [ ]. In addition to physical symptoms, it also leads to psychosocial consequences, as children often face social embarrassment and isolation, withdraw from peer activities, and experience a lower quality of life that impacts both their development and family dynamics [ ]. The management of pediatric OAB follows a stepwise approach, starting with conservative measures such as behavioral interventions and lifestyle modifications before pharmacological interventions [ ]. When non-pharmacological methods fail, antimuscarinic agents are the primary medical treatment [ ]. Despite their efficacy, they are limited by anticholinergic side effects such as dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and headache [ ]. Mirabegron stimulates β3 receptors in the detrusor muscle, inducing relaxation during storage, which improves bladder capacity and decreases contractility [ ]. In contrast to antimuscarinics, it maintains normal voiding function and reduces residual urine [ ]. A comprehensive pooled analysis of three large phase III studies revealed that mirabegron significantly improved incontinence and micturition, with efficacy comparable to that of antimuscarinics and superior tolerability in adults with OAB [ ]. Mirabegron has been shown in multiple trials to be effective in treating OAB in adults and was adopted by the NICE guidelines in 2013 [ – ]. As a β3 agonist, it also appears safe and effective in children with OAB, improving urodynamic parameters and clinical symptoms, and provides an alternative for refractory or antimuscarinic-intolerant patients [ , ]. Previous studies comparing mirabegron and solifenacin in paediatric OAB patients have shown varying results. Soliman et al. reported that both agents are effective, with mirabegron showing better tolerability [ ]. Kim et al. reported similar efficacy and safety, whereas Mansour et al. suggested that mirabegron may offer superior outcomes with fewer adverse effects [ , ]. However, no systematic review has compared these agents in children. Therefore, this review aimed to evaluate evidence comparing the efficacy and safety of mirabegron versus solifenacin in children with OAB, aiming to offer insights that can guide clinical decisions and optimize treatment. Methods Protocol This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ ]. The study protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the registration number CRD420251129236. Search strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted across four electronic databases: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, up to September 2, 2025. No date restrictions were applied; however, the search was limited to studies published in English. The search strategy combined keywords and medical subject headings related to the pediatric population, overactive bladder, mirabegron, and solifenacin. The detailed search strategy for databases is provided in Appendix 1. Eligibility criteria Studies eligible for this review included randomized controlled trials, clinical trials, prospective or retrospective cohort studies, and case‒control studies that directly compared mirabegron and solifenacin as monotherapies. The study population was children and adolescents (≤ 18 years) diagnosed with non-neurogenic OAB. Conversely, studies were excluded if they were case reports, case series, reviews, or editorials. Additionally, studies without a direct comparator arm or those focusing exclusively on neurogenic bladder populations were not included. Outcome definition The efficacy outcome was treatment response, although its definition varied across the included studies. Mansour et al. defined efficacy as a ≥ 50% reduction in the baseline Dysfunctional Voiding Scoring System (DVSS) score [ ]. Soliman et al. used a similar threshold, defining success as a > 50% improvement based on a symptom relief questionnaire [ ] In contrast, Kim et al. defined a response as a ≥ 90% reduction in symptoms based on patient and parent reports [ ]. The safety outcome was assessed as the occurrence of any treatment-related adverse events. Study selection Studies imported into the Rayyan web application for systematic reviews [ ]. After duplicate records were manually removed, two reviewers independently and blindly screened the titles and abstracts of the remaining articles to assess their relevance. The full texts of the studies that met our predetermined inclusion criteria were subsequently screened. Any disagreements during the selection process were resolved by discussion and agreement with a third reviewer. The flow diagram was generated via the PRISMA2020 R package and Shiny app [ ]. Quality assessment and publication

safety outcome was assessed as the occurrence of any treatment-related adverse events. Study selection Studies imported into the Rayyan web application for systematic reviews [ ]. After duplicate records were manually removed, two reviewers independently and blindly screened the titles and abstracts of the remaining articles to assess their relevance. The full texts of the studies that met our predetermined inclusion criteria were subsequently screened. Any disagreements during the selection process were resolved by discussion and agreement with a third reviewer. The flow diagram was generated via the PRISMA2020 R package and Shiny app [ ]. Quality assessment and publication bias The quality of the included studies was independently assessed by two blinded reviewers, with any disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Randomized controlled trials were evaluated with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2 (RoB 2) [ ] which covers seven domains: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and investigators, blinding of outcome assessors, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential biases. Each domain is rated as “low risk,” “high risk,” or “some concerns.” Non-randomized studies, including cohort designs, were assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) [ ]. Three areas are evaluated: selection of study groups (up to four stars), comparability of groups (up to two stars), and ascertainment of exposure or outcome (up to three stars). Based on total scores, studies were categorized as high, moderate, or low quality, with higher scores indicating better methodological rigor. Statistical analysis Dichotomous outcomes (treatment response and the incidence of adverse events) were analyzed using the Risk Ratio (RR) with its 95% confidence interval (CI) to estimate effects. Due to the expected clinical and methodological heterogeneity among the included studies, a random-effects model was employed for meta-analysis. Statistical heterogeneity was measured with Higgins’ I² test. According to established guidelines, an I² value of 0–40% indicates insignificant heterogeneity, 30–60% suggests moderate heterogeneity, 50–90% reflects substantial heterogeneity, and 75–100% shows considerable heterogeneity [ ]. To test the robustness of the results and determine the influence of each study on the overall estimate, a sensitivity analysis was performed by removing one study at a time and reanalyzing the data. All statistical analyses for this review were conducted using Review Manager software Version 5.3 [ ]. Results Study selection As shown in Fig. , our search strategy yielded a total of 222 studies from four databases. After eliminating 55 duplicate records, 167 studies remained for screening. Of these, 162 were excluded based on title and abstract screening. After full-text screening, three studies were included in the review, involving a total of 246 patients, with 116 patients treated with mirabegron and 130 patients treated with solifenacin. Baseline characteristics The total sample size across the included studies was 116 patients in the mirabegron group and 130 patients in the solifenacin group. The mean age (SD) was 9.44 years (1.97) for the Mirabegron group and 8.55 years (2.21) for the Solifenacin group, with an overall range of 5–15 years across included studies. Overall, 41.8% of the participants were male. The Mansour and Soliman studies followed both treatment groups for 12 weeks, whereas Kim et al. followed Mirabegron patients for 34 weeks and Solifenacin patients for 28 weeks. The baseline characteristics of the included studies are shown in Table . Clinical characteristics and outcomes Table outlined the characteristics and clinical outcomes of pediatric patients with OAB treated with mirabegron versus solifenacin across three studies: Kim et al., Mansour et al., and Soliman et al. Mansour et al. and Soliman et al. were single-blind randomized controlled trials (RCTs), whereas Kim et al. was an observational study. All studies included pediatric patients with idiopathic non-neurogenic OAB aged from 5 to 15 years. The intervention consisted of a daily single dose of mirabegron at 50 mg, with weight-adjusted dosing in Mansour et al., whereas the comparator was a daily single dose of solifenacin at 5 mg across all studies. Fewer adverse events were consistently associated with mirabegron than with solifenacin. The efficacy outcomes showed that Mirabegron was comparable to solifenacin in Kim et al. and Soliman et al., whereas Mansour et al. reported greater efficacy for Mirabegron. Risk-of-bias assessment and publication bias The observational study by Kim et al., evaluated with the NOS, scored 7 out of 9 stars, indicating good overall quality. It received the maximum score for selection, one star for comparability, and two stars for outcome assessment. Among the randomized controlled trials, Mansour et al. demonstrated a low overall risk of bias across all domains, with no concerns regarding randomization, deviations from intervention, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, or selective reporting. In contrast, Soliman et al. was judged to have a high overall risk of bias, primarily due to issues with the randomization process, deviations from the intended intervention, and selective reporting of outcomes, while outcome measurement

with the NOS, scored 7 out of 9 stars, indicating good overall quality. It received the maximum score for selection, one star for comparability, and two stars for outcome assessment. Among the randomized controlled trials, Mansour et al. demonstrated a low overall risk of bias across all domains, with no concerns regarding randomization, deviations from intervention, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, or selective reporting. In contrast, Soliman et al. was judged to have a high overall risk of bias, primarily due to issues with the randomization process, deviations from the intended intervention, and selective reporting of outcomes, while outcome measurement and data completeness were considered low risk. Efficacy outcomes The pooled analysis of all three studies indicated that mirabegron was not statistically superior to solifenacin in achieving treatment response (RR = 1.11, 95% CI: 0.92–1.33, p = 0.28). Notably, substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies (I² = 58%, p = 0.09), arising from differing treatment-response definitions. However, Explanatory sensitivity was done by excluding the study by Soliman et al. (assessed as high risk of bias), the pooled estimate from the remaining two studies demonstrated a statistically significant benefit of mirabegron over solifenacin (RR = 1.24, 95% CI: 1.04–1.47, p = 0.02), and in this sensitivity analysis heterogeneity was fully resolved (I² = 0%) Fig. . Safety outcome As shown in Fig. , mirabegron was associated with a 56% lower risk of adverse events than solifenacin. The incidence of adverse events was 16.4% (19/116) for mirabegron and 35.4% (46/130) for solifenacin. The pooled risk ratio was 0.44 (95% CI 0.28–0.70; Z = 3.52, p = 0.0004), with negligible heterogeneity (I² = 0%). All three studies favoured mirabegron, with Soliman et al. and Mansour et al. contributing the most to the pooled effect. Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis summarized current evidence comparing the efficacy and safety of mirabegron and solifenacin in children with non-neurogenic OAB. Across three studies involving 246 patients, pooled analysis suggested no difference in treatment response. However, after excluding the high-risk study, the sensitivity analysis suggested that mirabegron had superior efficacy. This finding is based on only two studies with a combined sample size of 117 patients and should be interpreted cautiously as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Notably, mirabegron demonstrated a 56% lower risk of treatment-related adverse events, indicating a better short-term safety profile. The studies included children ranging from 5 to 15 years of age (mean age 6–10 years), which is typical for pediatric OAB populations [ ]. At baseline, symptom burden was similar across groups, with common OAB features such as urgency, frequency, daytime incontinence, and nocturnal enuresis [ , , ]. Differences in study design may explain variations in reported efficacy. For example, Kim et al. defined response as ≥ 90% symptom improvement, while Mansour and Soliman defined response as ≥ 50% symptom improvement [ – ]. This variability highlights the need for standardized outcome measures in future pediatric OAB research. Our results showed that mirabegron might be effective as solifenacin in children with OAB, which is consistent with findings in adults. Wang et al. reported no significant differences between mirabegron 50 mg and solifenacin 5 mg in reducing incontinence, urgency, or micturition frequency [ ]. These results align with those of a trial conducted by Batista et al. and studies by Jamil et al. and Scaldazza et al., which reported comparable symptom relief [ – ]. Likewise, Soliman et al. and Kim et al. found no superiority of either drug in pediatric populations [ , ]. Conversely, Mansour et al. reported higher response rates with mirabegron [ ]. Solifenacin blocks M3 muscarinic receptors, while mirabegron stimulates β3-adrenergic receptors, but both drugs lead to detrusor muscle relaxation during bladder storage [ , , ]. This shared physiological effect may explain their comparable efficacy in reducing urgency, frequency, and incontinence. However, variations in results across studies likely arise from differences in patient populations, baseline symptom severity, prior treatment exposure, and the tools used for symptom evaluation. However, given the limited number of included studies and small sample sizes, these findings should be considered preliminary. Larger, adequately powered pediatric RCTs are needed to determine whether any subtle differences in efficacy exist between mirabegron and solifenacin. Beyond pharmacologic mechanisms and studies’ variability, a crucial clinical consideration is the overlap between OAB and dysfunctional voiding [ ]. These conditions often coexist, with nearly half of patients with dysfunctional voiding requiring treatment for OAB, and vice versa [ ]. Although studies in our meta-analysis excluded children with known dysfunctional voiding, diagnostic overlap could contribute to variable treatment responses and should prompt clinicians to evaluate concomitant dysfunctional voiding when OAB treatments yield incomplete responses. Although studies in our meta-analysis excluded children with known dysfunctional voiding, diagnostic overlap could contribute to variable treatment responses and should prompt clinicians to evaluate concomitant dysfunctional voiding when OAB treatments yield incomplete responses. In terms of safety, our analysis suggested that mirabegron was associated with a significantly lower incidence of adverse events than solifenacin in children, with overall event rates of 16.4% versus 35.4%, representing a relative reduction of approximately 56%. Adverse events associated with solifenacin were most commonly constipation, dry mouth, and headache, whereas mirabegron was associated with fewer and generally milder effects, such as headache or transient gastrointestinal discomfort. These results are consistent with previous studies in adults, where anticholinergic agents like solifenacin are consistently linked to constipation and dry mouth, while mirabegron demonstrates a more favourable safety profile [ – ]. This difference is likely due to their pharmacological mechanisms, as solifenacin has anticholinergic effects that affect multiple organs, whereas mirabegron acts as a β3-adrenergic receptor agonist, selectively targeting detrusor smooth muscle with limited systemic spillover or off-target effects that are common with solifenacin [ , ]. The better tolerability of mirabegron is important in pediatrics, where side effects often cause treatment discontinuation [ ]. By lowering this risk, mirabegron may support adherence and symptom control, potentially offering a safer short-term option for treating OAB in children within the limitations of current evidence. Our findings related to non-neurogenic (idiopathic) OAB, for which neither mirabegron nor solifenacin has pediatric approval. Mirabegron received FDA approval in 2021 for neurogenic detrusor overactivity (NDO) in children ≥ 3 years, but remains off-label for idiopathic pediatric OAB [ ]. Similarly, solifenacin has pediatric approval only for NDO [ ]. Nevertheless, both agents are commonly prescribed in practice, highlighting the need for systematic evidence synthesis to guide decision-making without formal regulatory guidance. Current treatments and future perspectives Antimuscarinic agents are the primary treatment for pediatric OAB, with oxybutynin and tolterodine being the only approved medications [ ]. However, their limited uroselectivity and associated adverse effects contribute to poor treatment persistence (11.8%) and high discontinuation rates (32%) [ , ]. Concerns have also been raised regarding neurodevelopmental safety, particularly because oxybutynin crosses the blood–brain barrier. Nonetheless, current evidence has not demonstrated measurable cognitive harm [ , ]. However, long-term neurodevelopmental data remain limited. Considering these limitations, β3-adrenoceptor agonists have emerged as alternative therapies [ ]. Despite their therapeutic potential, cardiovascular safety remains a key concern, as Chapple et al. reported increases in heart rate and blood pressure, necessitating regular monitoring [ ]. To optimize efficacy while mitigating dose-related adverse effects, dual therapy has been explored. In pediatric overactive bladder, this approach combines an antimuscarinic, typically solifenacin, with the β3-agonist mirabegron to enhance bladder relaxation through complementary mechanisms [ ]. In adults, combination therapy has demonstrated greater efficacy than monotherapy [ – ]. Similarly, in children refractory to antimuscarinics, add-on mirabegron improved bladder capacity and continence with generally mild side effects [ , ]. Overall, dual therapy appears promising and well-tolerated; however, randomized pediatric trials are still needed. Beyond established therapies, Vibegron is a highly selective β3-adrenoceptor agonist with a potentially more favorable cardiovascular profile than mirabegron [ ]. A comprehensive adult review confirmed vibegron’s high β3-AR selectivity, effective symptom relief, minimal cardiovascular effects, and favorable tolerability that may support better long-term adherence [ ]. Kato et al. reported the first pediatric case of vibegron use for anticholinergic-resistant neurogenic detrusor overactivity, demonstrating improved bladder compliance and resolution of detrusor overactivity on urodynamic assessment [ ]. Subsequently, Kitta et al. provided the first urodynamic evaluation of vibegron in children and adolescents with idiopathic OAB, documenting improvements in both subjective symptoms and lower urinary tract function [ ]. These findings suggest that vibegron may be a promising option for children refractory to anticholinergics, although larger prospective studies are required to confirm its safety and long-term efficacy. In parallel with pharmacologic therapies, high-dose vitamin D supplementation (VDS) has been explored as a safe and accessible strategy for pediatric OAB. In a three-arm randomized clinical trial, Chen et al. demonstrated that high-dose VDS (2400 IU/day) combined with standard urotherapy resulted in greater improvements in voiding frequency compared with solifenacin plus urotherapy or urotherapy alone, with an excellent safety profile [ ]. These findings suggest that vitamin D may influence bladder function and that baseline vitamin D status could modify treatment response; however, larger studies are needed to confirm mechanisms, optimal dosing, and long-term outcomes. When pharmacological therapy is ineffective or poorly tolerated, third-line therapies like intradetrusor botulinum toxin A (BoNT-A) injections and percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS) are considered, though their pediatric use is limited by practical constraints [ – ]. BoNT-A is FDA-approved for pediatric neurogenic detrusor overactivity and benefits refractory OAB, with response rates of around 50% [ – ]. However, its effects last only 6–9 months, requiring repeat injections under anesthesia, increasing cost risks, procedure complications, and family burden [ ]. PTNS has shown efficacy, with improved durability versus antimuscarinic therapy alone, but requires weekly 30-minute office sessions plus maintenance therapy, while pediatric in-home protocols remain unstudied [ , ]. Although clinically effective, the requirement for repeated in-office treatments may limit accessibility and long-term adherence in children, highlighting the need for validated home-based neuromodulation strategies. For this reason, focus has shifted toward noninvasive neuromodulation strategies. A systematic review and meta-analysis of eight randomized trials found that parasacral transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) produced 3.34-fold higher complete response rates than standard therapy, without significant adverse effects [ ] Lin et al. reported that transcutaneous pelvic floor magnetic stimulation combined with voiding training achieved superior outcomes compared with voiding training alone in children with OAB [ ]. Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) is being explored in refractory pediatric cases. Although sacral neuromodulation is not FDA-approved for children under 16 years for urological indications, off-label pediatric studies have demonstrated overall symptom improvement in approximately 68% of patients and complete resolution in 39%, with concurrent improvements in quality of life and urodynamic findings; however, these benefits must be weighed against notable complication and reoperation rates [ ]. SNM may be considered a viable third-line option in carefully selected pediatric patients, while emphasizing the need for standardized protocols and larger multicenter studies to define long-term efficacy. The findings of this meta-analysis should be considered preliminary due to several key limitations. Only three studies met the inclusion criteria, and with relatively small sample sizes, which limits the statistical power and generalizability of our findings. The substantial variability among the included studies in terms of design, follow-up duration, and definitions of treatment response constitutes a major methodological limitation. This inconsistency not only undermines confidence in the pooled efficacy estimate but also likely contributed significantly to the observed heterogeneity. Importantly, the safety conclusions of this meta-analysis are limited to short-term adverse events observed during follow-up periods of 12–34 weeks. Therefore, the long-term safety of mirabegron and solifenacin in the pediatric population cannot be determined based on the currently available evidence. Furthermore, none of the studies evaluated cognitive outcomes, which is an important factor when comparing antimuscarinic and non-antimuscarinic therapies in children [ ]. Finally, because the included studies enrolled children aged 5–15 years, the findings may not be generalizable to infants, toddlers, or older adolescents. Despite these limitations, our study is the first meta-analysis to compare mirabegron and solifenacin in the treatment of pediatric OAB directly. The results suggest that mirabegron may be an effective and safer alternative; however, further high-quality, randomized controlled trials with standardized outcome definitions and longer follow-up periods are needed. Conclusions This systematic review and meta-analysis summarized evidence comparing mirabegron and solifenacin in pediatric OAB. The pooled data suggested comparable efficacy, with mirabegron showing a favorable short-term adverse event profile. However, given the few included studies and limited sample size, these findings are preliminary. Larger, multicenter RCTs with standardized outcomes and longer follow-up are needed to confirm these observations and inform clinical decisions. Supplementary Information Supplementary Material 1.
